title: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribes to Alleviate the Burden of Clinical Documentation
pub: NEJM Catalyst Innovations in Care Delivery 5(3)
author: Aaron A. Tierney · Gregg Gayre · Brian Hoberman · Britt Mattern · Manuel Ballesca · Patricia Kipnis · Vincent Liu · Kristine Lee

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core augmentation-and-redesign proposition and adds a concrete large-scale implementation case: TPMG paired ambient AI with training, peer support, vendor iteration and monitoring, while retaining clinician editing and ongoing quality oversight. Its healthcare setting limits direct legal-sector generalisation, but materially strengthens the operating-model and verification claims.
qs: The implementation process leveraged TPMG’s extensive experience in large-scale technology instantiation and integration incorporating multiple training formats, _at-the-elbow_ peer support, patient-facing materials, rapid-cycle upgrades with the technology vendor, and ongoing monitoring.

Despite this technology’s early promise, careful and ongoing attention must be paid to ensure that the technology supports clinicians while also optimizing ambient AI scribe output for accuracy, relevance, and alignment in the physician–patient relationship.

kp.k: Documentation burden harms clinicians and patient relationships
kp.d: In this medical-domain commentary, published February 21, 2024, the authors identify EHR documentation as a major driver of physician burnout and dissatisfaction. They argue that clerical work during encounters also interferes with empathetic communication and care.
qs: Clinical documentation in the electronic health record (EHR) has become increasingly burdensome for physicians and is a major driver of clinician burnout and dissatisfaction.
Time dedicated to clerical activities and data entry during patient encounters also negatively affects the patient–physician relationship by hampering effective and empathetic communication and care.

kp.k: Ambient scribes augment clinicians through real-time conversation processing
kp.d: The authors describe machine learning applied to conversations to provide real-time scribe-like capabilities. The technology uses a smartphone microphone to transcribe encounters without retaining audio recordings. Reduced documentation burden and improved encounters are presented as potential benefits, with the technology framed as augmenting clinicians.
qs: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes, which use machine learning applied to conversations to facilitate scribe-like capabilities in real time, has great potential to reduce documentation burden, enhance physician–patient encounters, and augment clinicians’ capabilities.
The technology leverages a smartphone microphone to transcribe encounters as they occur but does not retain audio recordings.

kp.k: Large-scale deployment generated substantial early use
kp.d: TPMG enabled the technology for 10,000 physicians and staff in October 2023 across diverse settings and specialties. Within 10 weeks, 3,442 physicians had used it in as many as 303,266 encounters. Of these users, 968 physicians enabled scribes in ≥100 encounters, and one enabled the tool in 1,210 encounters. These figures describe availability and actual use separately.
qs: To address the urgent and growing burden of data entry, in October 2023, The Permanente Medical Group (TPMG) enabled ambient AI technology for 10,000 physicians and staff to augment their clinical capabilities across diverse settings and specialties.

In 10 weeks since implementation, the ambient AI tool has been used by 3,442 TPMG physicians to assist in as many as 303,266 patient encounters across a wide array of medical specialties and locations.
In total, 968 physicians have enabled ambient AI scribes in ≥100 patient encounters, with one physician having enabled it to assist in 1,210 encounters.

kp.k: Implementation combined training, peer support, and iterative upgrades
kp.d: The deployment drew on TPMG’s previous large-scale technology implementation experience. Its reported components included multiple training formats, at-the-elbow peer support, patient-facing materials, rapid-cycle vendor upgrades, and ongoing monitoring.
qs: The implementation process leveraged TPMG’s extensive experience in large-scale technology instantiation and integration incorporating multiple training formats, _at-the-elbow_ peer support, patient-facing materials, rapid-cycle upgrades with the technology vendor, and ongoing monitoring.

kp.k: Users reported better interactions and less after-hours work
kp.d: The authors report favorable responses from physicians who used the service, including more personal and effective patient interactions and reduced after-hours clerical burden. Early patient feedback was also positive, with some patients reporting better physician interactions. These are reported experiences rather than quantified effects in the supplied abstract.
qs: The response from physicians who have used the ambient AI scribe service has been favorable; they cite the technology’s capability to facilitate more personal, meaningful, and effective patient interactions and to reduce the burden of after-hours clerical work.
In addition, early assessments of patient feedback have been positive, with some describing improved interaction with their physicians.

kp.k: Early quality assessment supports physician-edited AI documentation
kp.d: Early evaluation using an existing instrument for assessing human-generated scribe notes found high-quality AI-generated clinical documentation for physicians to edit. The finding concerns documentation quality within a clinician-editing workflow, not autonomous reliance on AI output; the supplied abstract gives no numerical quality scores.
qs: Early evaluation metrics, based on an existing tool that evaluates the quality of human-generated scribe notes, find that ambient AI use produces high-quality clinical documentation for physicians’ editing.

kp.k: Use was associated with reduced documentation and EHR time
kp.d: The authors report that statistical analyses after implementation linked AI scribe use with less time spent documenting and using the EHR. The supplied abstract describes an association and does not provide effect sizes, comparison groups, or detailed statistical methods.
qs: Further statistical analyses after AI scribe implementation also find that usage is linked with reduced time spent in documentation and in the EHR.

kp.k: Integration improvements and continuing accuracy oversight remain necessary
kp.d: The authors identify direct EHR integration, improved incorporation of medical interpretation, and individualized workflow personalization as areas needing enhancement. They qualify the technology’s early promise by calling for ongoing attention to output accuracy, relevance, clinician support, and alignment with the physician–patient relationship.
qs: Ongoing enhancements of the technology are needed and are focused on direct EHR integration, improved capabilities for incorporating medical interpretation, and enhanced workflow personalization options for individual users.

Despite this technology’s early promise, careful and ongoing attention must be paid to ensure that the technology supports clinicians while also optimizing ambient AI scribe output for accuracy, relevance, and alignment in the physician–patient relationship.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tierney and coauthors present ambient AI scribes as clinical augmentation that can reduce documentation burdens and improve physician–patient encounters, with early findings supporting this promise.
pts.d: This is a health-care source, not a claim about legal services. The authors describe real-time, conversation-based scribing through a smartphone microphone without retained audio recordings. They report that use is associated with less documentation and EHR time, that physicians report less after-hours clerical work and improved patient interactions, and that early quality evaluations find high-quality drafts for physicians to edit. The broader potential to enhance clinicians’ capabilities is framed as a promise rather than established comprehensive improvement. The source describes augmentation, not autonomous clinical practice or replacement of physicians, and does not report a measured reduction in burnout.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors offer implementation usage data, physician and patient feedback, early note-quality evaluation, and statistical associations with reduced documentation time.
pts.d: The substantive material supplied is the abstract; the full article is subscriber-only. At TPMG, 3,442 physicians used the tool in as many as 303,266 encounters over the first 10 weeks; 968 used it in at least 100 encounters and one in 1,210. These figures document uptake rather than quantify benefits. Physicians’ favorable reports and early patient feedback support the interaction and workload claims. Documentation quality was assessed using an existing instrument for human-generated scribe notes. The abstract reports statistical links to lower documentation and EHR time but provides no effect sizes, analytical design, comparison-group details, feedback sample sizes, or numerical quality scores. The time-saving finding is stated as an association, not a demonstrated causal effect. These are claims from Tierney and coauthors’ account of their organisation’s implementation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings concern the first 10 weeks following the October 2023 rollout, with benefits qualified by physician editing, implementation support, and continuing improvements.
pts.d: The article was published February 21, 2024, as specified in its publication history; the supplied page’s 2026 timestamp is not the article’s stated publication date. The authors repeatedly characterise results as early. Deployment incorporated training, at-the-elbow peer support, patient-facing materials, rapid vendor upgrades, and monitoring. They identify direct EHR integration, incorporation of medical interpretation, and personalised workflows as areas needing enhancement. They call for continuing attention to accuracy, relevance, and the physician–patient relationship. No timetable for completing enhancements or prediction of long-term benefits is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported beneficiaries are TPMG physicians and their patients across multiple specialties and settings; the organisation also undertakes implementation and monitoring work.
pts.d: Physicians receive assistance with clinical notes, retain an editing role, and report reduced after-hours clerical work and more meaningful patient interactions. Patients may receive more attentive communication, with some early respondents describing improved encounters. Access was enabled for 10,000 physicians and staff, but the reported usage count specifically concerns physicians; separate effects on nonphysician staff are not supplied. TPMG and its technology vendor support training, upgrades, monitoring, and workflow improvements. The source makes no concrete claims about employment displacement, financial returns, legal markets, or effects on human-scribe jobs.
